title: Forms of Stratification
description: Caste, estate and class: how societies rank people, and what the ranking costs

concepts.title: What Stratification Means
concepts.contentHtml:
Start with a number. In England between 2018 and 2020, men living in the most deprived tenth of neighbourhoods could expect to live 73.5 years, while men in the least deprived tenth could expect 83.2.1 The Office for National Statistics put the gap at 9.7 years for men and 7.9 years for women.2 The gap in years lived in good health was wider still: 19.3 years for women and 18.6 for men.3 Nobody chose those outcomes, and they are not random. They follow a pattern.

That pattern is what sociologists call social stratification: the ranking of groups into layers that receive unequal shares of what people value, such as money, power, respect, safety and long life. Three features separate stratification from mere difference. It is structured, attached to positions rather than to individual quirks. It is persistent, lasting for decades. And it is inherited, because parents pass much of their position to their children.

A good first question about any system is how positions are handed out. An ascribed status comes with birth: a caste, a noble title, often race or sex. An achieved status is won through effort, skill or luck: a medical degree, a business, an election. Every real society mixes the two. The interesting questions are how much of each, and how often a status that looks achieved, like a place at a top university, quietly depends on one that was ascribed.

The odds that a position gives you of getting the good things in life and avoiding the bad ones are called your life chances. This topic follows them through seven lessons: the main kinds of stratification system, the theories that explain them, how class and inequality are measured, how mobility works, how advantage is passed on, and how poverty is counted at home and across the world.

concepts.title: Closed Systems: Caste and Estate
concepts.contentHtml:
The most closed stratification systems are caste systems, and Hindu India is the defining case. Castes are ranked on a scale of ritual purity, with the top places reserved for castes that avoid behaviour seen as polluting.1 Sociologists describe four parts: a hierarchy of hereditary groups, closure rules that forbid marriage and mobility between castes, strict segregation in work and social contact, and a religious ideology that makes the order seem legitimate.

Caste is not just history. In a survey of 29,999 Indian adults, interviewed face to face between November 2019 and March 2020,2 the Pew Research Center found that nearly all Indians identify with a caste, whatever their religion.3 About 68% placed themselves in lower castes, and just 4% said they were Brahmin, the priestly caste at the top.4 Most people did not think caste discrimination was widespread, yet social life stayed inside caste lines: 24% said all their close friends were from their own caste, and 64% said it was very important to stop women in their community marrying into another caste.5

An estate system draws its lines in law rather than ritual. Pre-revolutionary France had three orders: clergy, nobility and commons. The first two were largely exempt from tax, so most of the burden fell on the Third Estate, which made up somewhere between 90% and 98% of the population.6 When Louis XVI summoned the Estates-General in 1789, the Third Estate was given 578 deputies against 303 for the clergy and 282 for the nobility.7 But if each estate voted as a bloc, as in 1614, the two privileged orders could always outvote it. The dispute ended with the Third Estate breaking away to form a National Assembly, generally seen as the start of the French Revolution.

Estates were less sealed than castes. Feudal lords held legal title to their serfs' labour, yet in feudalism's early, transitional period access to the nobility was not legally restricted to nobles' children, and marriage across estates was not formally forbidden.

concepts.title: Class: Open in Law, Sticky in Life
concepts.contentHtml:
Industrial societies swept the estates away. In the class systems that replaced them, legal orders gave way to purely economic groups, and hereditary closure rules gave way to processes that are, on paper, meritocratic.1 No law stops a miner's daughter becoming a judge. Your class depends on your place in the economy, chiefly your job, your property and your earnings, not on a title you were born with.

Formally open is not the same as equally open. The life-expectancy gap you met at the start of this lesson arose in a class society, and later lessons show how strongly class position still passes from parents to children. That gap between promise and practice is why one word dominates modern arguments about class: meritocracy, a society that hands out positions according to talent and effort.

Here is a surprise. The word began as a warning. By tradition, Michael Young is credited with coining it for his 1958 satire,2 whose full title is The Rise of the Meritocracy, 1870–2033. In fact the term had appeared in print two years earlier, in essays by Jean Floud, Alan Fox and Paul Lamartine Yates.3 All four were English academics who moved in similar left-wing circles, and for them the word had a negative connotation. Young's own feelings about the idea were mixed.

Keep three questions in mind for every system you meet in this topic:

  • Allocation: are positions handed out by birth, by law or by the market?
  • Movement: how often do people, or their children, change position?
  • Justification: what story makes the order seem fair: ritual purity, divine or legal order, or merit?

Caste, estate and class give different answers, but every stratified society has to answer all three.

title: Explaining Inequality: Function, Power and Closure
description: Marx and Weber applied, the Davis-Moore debate, and how groups close ranks

concepts.title: Marx and Weber, Applied
concepts.contentHtml:
Marx and Weber get a full treatment in the topic on classical sociological theory. Here you only need the tools they left for studying inequality. For Karl Marx, class is a relationship to the means of production. The basic cleavage under capitalism runs between capitalists, who own productive property, and workers, who must sell their labour power to live. On this view inequality is not a ladder of ranks but a relationship, in which one side's profit comes from the other side's work.

Max Weber agreed that property matters but split stratification into separate dimensions:

  • Class is your market situation: what you can sell in the labour market and how scarce it is. Skilled workers are privileged because they are in high demand, so Weber's model has many class cleavages, not two.1
  • A status group is a community that shares a style of life and treats its members as social equals, such as a nobility or an ethnic caste. Status can cut against money: Weber noted that status honour normally stands in sharp opposition to the pretensions of sheer property,2 which is how an old family can look down on a newly rich one.
  • Party is organised power, from political parties to pressure groups.

Later sociologists turned both traditions into tools for counting. Erik Olin Wright kept Marx's focus on exploitation but added contradictory class locations for people who sell their labour yet control work: managers have authority over workers, while professionals are semi-autonomous. Even so, his 1978 model described an American working class of about 46% of the labour force.3 The Weberian line runs to John Goldthorpe, whose scheme you will meet in Lesson 3.

The practical lesson is that the word class does different jobs in different arguments. When someone says class matters, or that it is dead, ask which they mean: ownership, market position, lifestyle and prestige, or power. The evidence for each is different.

concepts.title: Is Inequality Necessary? Davis, Moore and Tumin
concepts.contentHtml:
Functionalism, taught in the topic on modern sociological theory, asks what each social arrangement does for society as a whole. Applied to inequality, it produced the most famous argument in the field. In 1945 Kingsley Davis and Wilbert Moore argued that every society faces a motivational problem:1 it must persuade its most able people to train for, and conscientiously perform, its most important and difficult jobs. Their solution was a hierarchy of rewards. Unequal pay, prestige and power, they wrote, form an "unconsciously evolved device by which societies insure that the important positions are conscientiously filled by the most qualified persons".2

Notice two things. The device is unconscious: no elite designed it. And the argument justifies unequal positions, not unequal starting points. It also never says how much inequality is enough.

In 1953 Melvin Tumin took the argument apart, proposition by proposition.3 Who decides which jobs are functionally important? A factory's engineers may look more important than its labourers, but Tumin pointed out that in the long run its unskilled workforce is just as indispensable. More damaging, stratification itself limits the discovery of talent, because children born at the bottom may never get the training that would reveal their abilities.4 Tumin concluded that differential rewards could only be justified as functional where everyone with potential has genuinely equal access to recruitment and training.

Other critics added two points:

  • Circularity: the theory calls the best-rewarded roles the most important, then cites their rewards as evidence of their importance.5
  • Power: a 1959 critique noted that people in key positions can demand far more than they need to stay motivated,6 so rewards also reflect bargaining strength.

The debate never fully closed. In 1994 Gerhard Lenski argued that the wage levelling of communist states had made it hard to recruit and motivate highly skilled workers,7 giving the functionalist case new evidence from the socialist experiment.

concepts.title: Closing the Gates: Social Closure
concepts.contentHtml:
If functionalism sees rewards as payment for scarce talent, the conflict tradition sees them as the spoils of power. Its sharpest tool comes from Weber: social closure, the process by which groups devise and enforce rules of membership in order to improve their position by monopolistic tactics.1 Later sociologists such as Anthony Giddens and Frank Parkin built theories of class around it. Exclusionary rules, Parkin argued in 1979, let closed groups maximise their claims to rewards and opportunities.

Modern closure rarely says no outsiders allowed. It says qualified people only. There are no formal sanctions that stop workers crossing class lines, yet institutions such as private property and union rules are quite effective at limiting mobility within a career and between generations. Theorists in this tradition use the economist's term rent: excess earnings secured by limiting access to positions, which artificially restricts the supply of qualified labour.2 One test asks whether skilled workers' lifetime earnings exceed unskilled workers' by more than the cost of their training.

Occupational licensing is a measurable case. In a national survey designed by Morris Kleiner and Alan Krueger and published in 2009, 29% of American employees were fully licensed by government,3 and licensing was associated with about 14% higher wages.4 Read that finding carefully. Defenders of licensing argue that it protects the public from unqualified practitioners, so part of the premium may reward real quality. Closure theorists reply that entry requirements also shrink supply and push up pay. The data show the premium; on their own they cannot say how much of it is protection and how much is closure.

Closure explains how inequality survives formal equality. A rule that applies to everyone, such as a requirement for a degree, long training or an unpaid apprenticeship, can still favour those who arrive with money, time and connections. Lesson 6 follows these gates in detail, from child-rearing to university admissions.

title: Measuring Class: Schemes, Censuses and Surveys
description: Goldthorpe's employment relations, the NS-SEC, and the Great British Class Survey row

concepts.title: Goldthorpe: Class as an Employment Relationship
concepts.contentHtml:
To study class with numbers you need a rule that sorts millions of people into categories. The most influential rule in European sociology is the Goldthorpe schema, developed by John Goldthorpe from 1980 onwards and used with Robert Erikson in The Constant Flux (1992), their study of class mobility in industrial societies. It is Weberian in spirit: it classifies people by the kind of employment relationship their job involves, not by income or prestige.

Two ideal types anchor the scheme:

  • In a service relationship, the employee renders service to the employer in return for both immediate rewards, such as a salary, and long-term or prospective benefits, such as security and career opportunities.1
  • In a labour contract, the employee gives discrete amounts of labour in return for a wage calculated on the amount of work done or time worked.2

Intermediate jobs mix the two. Employers, the self-employed and people who have never worked sit in separate categories, because they have no ordinary employment contract at all.

Why judge class by contracts? Because contracts shape life chances. They differ in the source of income, economic security and prospects of advancement, and in where a job sits in systems of authority and control at work. When Britain's statisticians chose a basis for their official classification, they picked the Goldthorpe schema because it is accepted internationally and conceptually clear,3 and because it had been reasonably validated as a predictor of health and other outcomes.

Notice what the scheme leaves out. Two plumbers with the same earnings can sit in different classes, one running a small firm and one employed by a council, because their place in the labour market differs. Critics say a contract-based scheme misses wealth, culture and the very rich. Defenders reply that a class scheme should capture structural positions and then be tested on what it predicts, rather than building every advantage into its definition. That argument returns in this lesson's third concept.

concepts.title: The NS-SEC: Class in the Census
concepts.contentHtml:
Since 2001 the UK's official class measure has been the National Statistics Socio-economic Classification (NS-SEC). It was developed from the Goldthorpe schema and constructed to measure the employment relations and conditions of occupations.1 It classifies positions, not people: two people in the same job on the same kind of contract land in the same class, whatever their accent, savings or taste in music.

Its analytic version has eight classes:

  • 1. Higher managerial, administrative and professional occupations
  • 2. Lower managerial, administrative and professional occupations
  • 3. Intermediate occupations
  • 4. Small employers and own account workers
  • 5. Lower supervisory and technical occupations
  • 6. Semi-routine occupations
  • 7. Routine occupations
  • 8. Never worked and long-term unemployed

Census 2021 coded every usual resident aged 16 and over in England and Wales from their answers about economic activity, occupation and employment history. The largest group was class 2, at 19.9% (9.7 million people),2 and class 1 held 13.1% (6.4 million).3 Intermediate occupations made up 11.4%, small employers and own account workers 10.6%, lower supervisory and technical occupations 5.4%, semi-routine occupations 11.4%, routine occupations 12.1%, and the never worked and long-term unemployed 8.5%, with full-time students another 7.7%. A third of adults now sit in the two managerial and professional classes, a legacy of what the Social Mobility Commission calls the great expansion of the professional classes in the 1960s and 1970s.

The NS-SEC is more than bookkeeping. Its designers say it was not built to produce stronger statistical associations than older schemes, but to make them easier to explain.4 Because each class is defined by real features of work and market situation, researchers can trace how class links to outcomes such as health through intervening variables, instead of just reporting a correlation.

concepts.title: The Great British Class Survey and Its Critics
concepts.contentHtml:
In January 2011 BBC Lab UK launched an online questionnaire, designed with the sociologists Mike Savage and Fiona Devine, about income, house value, savings, cultural and leisure activities and the occupations of friends. More than 161,000 people took part, making it the largest study of class in the UK.1 Drawing on Bourdieu, the team scored people on economic, social and cultural capital, and in 2013 they announced that Britain now has seven classes:

  • Elite: the most privileged, with the highest levels of all three capitals.
  • Established middle class: the largest group, at 25%.
  • Technical middle class: prosperous but socially isolated and culturally apathetic.
  • New affluent workers and emergent service workers: younger groups with middling or low incomes but active social and cultural lives.
  • Traditional working class: 14%, low on all capitals, with the oldest average age, 66.
  • Precariat: 15%, the poorest and most deprived.

Supporters said the survey caught two groups that class analysis focused on the middle and working classes had missed: an elite and a precariat. Critics were fierce. Internet surveys suffer from self-selection: participants were predominantly drawn from well-educated groups,2 so the team ran a second, identical survey with the polling firm GfK. Colin Mills of Oxford pointed out in 2014 that the seven classes therefore came from a latent profile model estimated almost entirely on that quota sample of 1,026 people,3 with the 161,400 web responses entered as a single case. He wrote that the project had a mountain of highly self-selected poor quality data sitting on top of a mole hill of (slightly) better quality data. On his reading, the elite could be 3% of the population or 9%.4

The deeper dispute is about what class is. Goldthorpe's tradition defines class by employment relations and then tests what it predicts. The survey built cultural and social capital into the definition, so, as Mills put it, the typology cannot explain differences in those capitals: they are built into the definition of the typology itself.

title: Income, Wealth and How Inequality Is Measured
description: Flows and stocks, the Gini and top shares, and the fight over Piketty's numbers

concepts.title: Income and Wealth: Flow and Stock
concepts.contentHtml:
Two words are often used as if they meant the same thing. Income is a flow: what comes in over a period, from wages, benefits, rents, interest and profits. Wealth is a stock: what you own at a moment, such as a house, a pension, savings and shares, minus your debts. A newly qualified doctor can have a high income and negative wealth; a retired farmer can have little income and a valuable farm.

Wealth is far more unequal than income, because it builds up over a lifetime and can be inherited. Britain's Wealth and Assets Survey shows how far. Between April 2018 and March 2020 the wealthiest 10% of households held 43% of all the wealth in Great Britain, while the bottom 50% held only 9%.1 To be in the richest 1% a household needed more than £3.6 million; the least wealthy 10% had £15,400 or less. On the Gini coefficient, where 0 means everyone has the same and 1 means one household has everything, the ONS put income at 0.36 in 2020 and wealth at around 0.6.2 Net financial wealth was the most unequal component, with a Gini of 0.89.

Age explains part of the gap, so sociologists handle wealth figures carefully. Wealth accumulates over decades, so the young look poor and people near retirement look rich even in a society without classes. The ONS found median wealth was highest, at £553,400, for households whose head was aged 55 to State Pension age.3 But age cannot explain why, as Lesson 6 shows, parents' wealth predicts the wealth of their adult children.

When you read a headline about inequality, ask which kind it means. The Political Economy topic adds a third measure, consumption, which tends to be the least concentrated of the three. Income, wealth and consumption tell different stories, and much public confusion comes from mixing them up.

concepts.title: Reading the Gini, and Looking at the Top
concepts.contentHtml:
You met the Gini coefficient and the Lorenz curve in the economics topics. Sociologists use them constantly, but with two worries. A Gini squeezes a whole distribution into one number, so two very different societies can share it: one where the middle is hollowing out, another where the top is pulling away. And, as the Public Economics topic notes, it is relatively insensitive to what happens at the very top. Britain's Department for Work and Pensions reports that income inequality measured by the Gini has been broadly stable since the financial year ending 2011.1 That tells you inequality stopped changing, not where it settled.

Measuring the top needs different data, because the very rich are rare in surveys. Thomas Piketty and Emmanuel Saez turned to tax returns. In a study published in 2003 they built series of top income shares for the United States from 1913 to 1998 and found a U-shaped pattern over the century.2 Concentration was high before the First World War, collapsed through the Depression and the Second World War, then climbed again. They argued that the shocks capital owners suffered in those decades had lasting effects, and that steep progressive taxation slowed the rebuilding of great fortunes.

Later work with Gabriel Zucman tried to account for all of national income, including income that never appears on a tax form, such as employer-provided benefits. Their distributional national accounts found that average pre-tax income per American adult grew 60% after 1980, while the income of the bottom half stagnated at about $16,000 a year.3 In 1980 the top 1% earned on average 27 times as much as the bottom 50%; in their latest figures, 81 times as much.4

Top-share series changed public debate, because they showed something the Gini had blurred: the rise in American inequality after 1980 was concentrated at the very top. The next concept asks how solid those numbers are.

concepts.title: Piketty and His Critics
concepts.contentHtml:
Thomas Piketty's Capital in the Twenty-First Century (2013) turned top-share data into a theory. As the Political Economy topic explains, his central claim is that when the return on capital, r, exceeds the growth rate of the economy, g, inherited wealth tends to grow faster than incomes, so the equalising mid-twentieth century was the exception, not the rule. Sociologists find the argument attractive because it puts inheritance, a classic mechanism of stratification, back at the centre.

The critics come from two directions. The first is theoretical. Daron Acemoglu and James Robinson argued in 2015 that general economic laws are unhelpful as a guide to the past or the future, because they ignore the central role of political and economic institutions and the way technology evolves. Using regressions across countries, they found that the gap between the interest rate and the growth rate does not appear to explain historical patterns of inequality, especially the share of income going to the top.1 Case histories of South Africa and Sweden, they argued, show that inequality cannot be understood without its institutions.

The second is about measurement. Gerald Auten and David Splinter argued in the Journal of Political Economy in 2024 that top shares based only on tax returns are biased by changes in the tax base, social changes and missing income sources. Correcting for these, they found that top income shares are lower and have increased less since 1980 than other studies using tax data.2 Once rising government transfers and more progressive taxes are counted, they found rising real incomes for all groups and little change in after-tax top shares.3

What survives? Both teams try to capture the income that tax returns miss, yet they reach different answers, so the size of the American rise in top shares is now a live measurement dispute rather than a settled fact. Few researchers doubt the broad shape: concentration fell in the mid-twentieth century and has risen since 1980. The arguments are over how much, over whether taxes and transfers offset it, and over whether r greater than g explains anything.

title: Social Mobility: Absolute, Relative and the Gatsby Curve
description: Counting movement between generations, the fading American dream, and what inequality does to mobility

concepts.title: Two Kinds of Mobility
concepts.contentHtml:
Ask whether a society is mobile and you are really asking two questions. Absolute mobility counts how many people end up higher or lower than their parents, in occupational class or real income. Relative mobility compares the chances of people from different starting points: it asks how much origin matters, not how many people moved.

The two can come apart. If an economy creates many more professional jobs, lots of working-class children will rise even if their chances relative to professionals' children do not change at all. This is structural mobility. In Britain the percentage of upwardly mobile people has always been higher than the percentage moving down,1 and the Social Mobility Commission's 2023 report attributes the surplus to increasing room at the top. The gap has narrowed recently, partly because the expansion of the professional classes in the 1960s and 1970s means more people now start near the top, with further to fall.

Relative mobility is measured with odds ratios. The Commission's own example uses housing. Among homeowners' children, 71% became homeowners and 29% renters;2 among renters' children the split was 46 to 54. Dividing one set of odds by the other gives an odds ratio of 2.9: the children of owners had nearly three times the odds of owning rather than renting. For occupations, adults in the UK with lower working-class parents are about three times as likely to be in a lower working-class job themselves (30%) as adults with higher professional parents (11%).3

In the mid-1970s Featherman, Jones and Hauser proposed that relative mobility is essentially the same everywhere, with countries differing only in structural change. Later research supported the weak form of their hypothesis, that most differences in overall mobility are structural, but found the strong form, identical relative chances everywhere, to be false.4 Erikson and Goldthorpe's The Constant Flux is a classic of this comparative work.

concepts.title: The Fading American Dream
concepts.contentHtml:
Measuring income mobility needs data that link parents to their grown-up children, which ordinary surveys rarely have. Raj Chetty and colleagues found a way round this. For their study "The Fading American Dream", published in Science in 2017, they combined historical census data with de-identified tax records and asked a simple question: what fraction of children earn more than their parents did, after adjusting for prices? The answer: rates of absolute mobility fell from approximately 90% for children born in 1940 to 50% for children born in the 1980s.1

Why the fall? Not mainly slower growth. The team found that higher GDP growth alone could not restore the old rates, whereas spreading growth across income groups as evenly as it had been for the 1940 cohort would reverse more than 70% of the decline.2 Absolute mobility fell because more of the growth went to the top.

Now the surprise. Relative mobility did not collapse. In a 2014 study Chetty, Nathaniel Hendren, Patrick Kline, Emmanuel Saez and Nicholas Turner found that percentile rank-based measures of mobility had remained extremely stable for Americans born from 1971 to 1993.3 A child starting at the bottom had much the same chance of climbing the rankings as one born in the 1970s. What changed was the distance between the rungs. Because inequality has risen, the consequences of the birth lottery, the parents you happen to be born to, are larger than they used to be.

Place matters as well as time. The same team showed that the probability of a child rising from the bottom fifth of the national income distribution to the top fifth was 4.4% in Charlotte but 12.9% in San Jose.4 High-mobility areas had less residential segregation, less income inequality, better primary schools, more social capital and greater family stability. These are correlations, not proof of cause, but they point to neighbourhoods as places where stratification is made.

concepts.title: The Great Gatsby Curve
concepts.contentHtml:
On 12 January 2012, Alan Krueger, then chairman of President Obama's Council of Economic Advisers, showed an audience at the Center for American Progress a scatter plot built on work by the economist Miles Corak. Each point was a country. One axis showed income inequality around the time children were growing up; the other showed the intergenerational income elasticity (IGE), a measure of how much of a parent's income advantage reappears in the child. The points clustered around an upward-sloping line, and Krueger named it the Great Gatsby Curve: more unequal countries show more persistence of income from one generation to the next.1

An IGE of 0.4, Krueger explained, means that if your parents earned 50% more than average, you can expect to earn 20% more than average.2 He offered a vivid comparison: the chance of rising from the bottom 10% of incomes to the top 10% is about the same as the chance that a father who is 5 feet 6 inches tall has a son over 6 feet 1. Reading forward from the curve, he forecast that the US IGE would rise from 0.47 to 0.56 for the next generation.3

The curve is a correlation across countries and should be read as one. Corak presented it as evidence about the drivers of opportunity,4 the ways families, labour markets and public policies shape children's chances differently in each country. It does not prove that inequality causes immobility. Krueger himself said nobody will know whether American mobility has worsened until today's children have grown up and finished their careers. And the tax data in the previous concept are a caution: rank mobility for Americans born up to 1993 had not yet fallen, even as inequality climbed.

The curve also overturned an old belief. Early in the twentieth century scholars thought the United States had especially high mobility,5 and Werner Sombart even blamed it for the weakness of American socialist parties. Krueger's data showed the reverse: parental income matters more for children's success in the US than in other developed economies.6

title: How Advantage Is Passed On
description: Bourdieu's capitals at work: child-rearing, elite schools, admissions, marriage and the class ceiling

concepts.title: Concerted Cultivation
concepts.contentHtml:
Money is the obvious inheritance, but Pierre Bourdieu argued that families also pass on cultural capital (knowledge, tastes and ways of speaking that institutions reward) and social capital (useful connections). The topic on modern sociological theory explains his concepts; this lesson watches them at work.

The best-known close-up is Annette Lareau's book Unequal Childhoods. Lareau began her data collection in 1989 and, between 1993 and 1995, intensively observed twelve families,1 Black and white, middle-class, working-class and poor. She found two distinct logics of child-rearing, and the split ran along class lines rather than racial ones.

  • Concerted cultivation: middle-class parents, whether Black or white, managed hectic schedules of organised activities designed to draw out their children's talents and skills.2
  • The accomplishment of natural growth: in working-class and poor families, a child's development was left to unfold spontaneously, as long as basic comfort, food and shelter were provided. These families often had plenty of time but little economic security.

Lareau did not call one style good and the other bad. Each brings its own benefits and its own drawbacks. The point, in Bourdieu's terms, is that schools and other institutions tend to treat middle-class habits as signs of ability. A child trained in concerted cultivation arrives already speaking the institution's language, and the advantage is recorded as merit.

Lareau went back. A decade later she revisited the same families and interviewed the original children as young adults,3 to see how social class shaped the transition to adulthood. Her study is small and qualitative, so it cannot measure how large these effects are across a whole country. Its value is in showing a mechanism: the everyday routines through which economic position turns into the dispositions that schools and employers reward.

concepts.title: Elite Schools and Elite Universities
concepts.contentHtml:
Education is meant to be the great leveller, but at the top it can work as a channel for inherited advantage. In 2019 the Sutton Trust and the Social Mobility Commission traced the backgrounds of more than 5,000 people in Britain's top jobs. Only 7% of the population attends independent, fee-paying schools, and roughly 1% graduates from Oxford or Cambridge. Yet two fifths (39%) of the elite group as a whole were privately educated, more than five times as many as the population at large,1 and about a quarter had Oxbridge degrees.

The concentration varied by field. It was highest among senior judges, 65% of whom went to independent schools and 71% to Oxbridge,2 followed by civil service permanent secretaries (59% privately educated) and the House of Lords (57%). Sport, particularly football, the arts and local government drew the fewest people from elite institutions.

In the United States the gate is admissions. In 2023 Raj Chetty, David Deming and John Friedman linked admissions records from several colleges to tax records and test scores. Children from families in the top 1% were more than twice as likely to attend an Ivy-Plus college (the Ivy League plus Stanford, MIT, Duke and Chicago) as middle-class children with comparable SAT or ACT scores.3 Two thirds of the gap came from higher admission rates at the same scores, driven by three things: preferences for the children of alumni, weight placed on non-academic credentials, and recruitment of athletes.4 Flagship public universities showed no such advantage for the rich.

Does the college matter? Comparing waitlisted applicants whose admission turned on idiosyncratic decisions, the team found that attending an Ivy-Plus college instead of the average flagship public college raised students' chances of reaching the top 1% of earners by 50%5 and almost tripled their chances of working at a prestigious firm. The three factors that favoured rich applicants were uncorrelated or negatively correlated with success after college, while test scores strongly predicted it. Admissions were turning family income into elite positions through criteria that did not predict later success.

concepts.title: Marriage, Wealth and the Class Ceiling
concepts.contentHtml:
Advantage also travels through marriage. Assortative mating is the tendency to pair with partners like yourself, in education and earnings. If high earners marry high earners, household incomes spread further apart than individual ones. In a 2014 paper Jeremy Greenwood and colleagues estimated that if American husbands and wives in 2005 had been matched at random, the Gini coefficient for household income would have fallen from 0.43 to 0.34,1 which would make sorting in marriage a major engine of inequality.

Then came a correction worth remembering whenever a striking number spreads. In a corrigendum filed in June 2015, the authors fixed two incorrect numbers. With random matching, the 2005 Gini falls only from 0.430 to 0.420, implying a small impact of sorting itself.2 Making couples sort as they had in 1960 barely moved it, from 0.430 to 0.429.3 The authors apologised for the mistakes and noted that studies using other methods and data had reached similar conclusions. What did matter, they found, was the rise in single and divorced households between 1960 and 2005.

Wealth passes on more directly. The Social Mobility Commission found in 2023 that for men a 10% increase in parents' wealth is associated with a 2.9% increase in their own, and for women with a 3.8% increase.4

Even reaching the top does not erase origins. Sam Friedman and Daniel Laurison call this the class ceiling. In a 2024 study using the Panel Study of Income Dynamics, they found that Americans from working-class backgrounds who rise into high-status occupations earn almost $20,000 a year less on average than colleagues from privileged backgrounds.5 Fewer college degrees explain part of that, but a gap of around $11,700 remains after accounting for education, race and other predictors of earnings. The gap was largest among white people, and it is distinct from the racial pay gap. Mobility, in other words, can get you through the door without giving you the same terms as those born inside.

title: Poverty and Global Inequality
description: Absolute and relative poverty lines, the World Bank's dollar a day, and the elephant curve debate

concepts.title: Drawing a Poverty Line
concepts.contentHtml:
Every poverty statistic hides a decision about where to draw the line. An absolute line fixes a standard of living and keeps it, adjusted only for prices. The official US measure is the classic case. Mollie Orshansky, a staff economist at the Social Security Administration, developed it in the mid-1960s:1 the cost of a minimum food diet, multiplied by three to cover other family expenses. In 2024 the official poverty rate fell 0.4 percentage points to 10.6%, or 35.9 million people.2

A relative line moves with the society around it. In his pioneering study Poverty in the United Kingdom, Peter Townsend argued that deprivation means more than material want: it also means exclusion from the ordinary patterns, customs and activities of society.3 Britain's main statistics follow that logic. A household is in relative low income if its income, adjusted for household size, is below 60% of that year's median.4 In the financial year ending 2024, 17% of people in the UK were below that line before housing costs, and 21% after them.

Even Britain's absolute measure is relative underneath: it counts people below 60% of the median for the financial year ending 2011, adjusted for inflation. A third approach asks the public. The 1983 Breadline Britain survey pioneered the consensual method: it tests items across food, clothing, housing, household goods, social and leisure activities and savings, keeps those that a majority of people regard as necessities, then counts households that cannot afford them. An enforced lack of three or more necessities is taken as a measure of deprivation poverty.5

The choice changes the picture. The Census Bureau's Supplemental Poverty Measure, first released in 2011, adds government benefits, taxes, work and medical expenses and local housing costs, and it first put the 2024 rate at 12.9% rather than 10.6%. In 2026 the Bureau of Labor Statistics re-released the thresholds behind it after finding coding errors, a reminder that even official lines get revised. Neither measure is the true one: each answers a different question.

concepts.title: A Dollar a Day, Then Three
concepts.contentHtml:
To count poverty across the world you need one yardstick for every country. In 1990 a group of researchers examined national poverty lines from some of the poorest countries and converted them into a common currency using purchasing power parities (PPPs), exchange rates built so that the same goods and services cost the same everywhere. In six very poor countries around the 1980s the national line came to about $1 per person per day in 1985 prices.1 That became the first dollar-a-day international poverty line.

The value has been revised as prices and data improve, but the idea has not changed: the line identifies people living in absolute monetary poverty by the standards of the world's poorest countries.2 In 2022 the World Bank set it at $2.15 a day in 2017 PPPs, the median national poverty line of 28 low-income countries. In June 2025 it moved to $3.00 in 2021 PPPs. The median of 23 low-income countries' lines came out at $3.04, Burkina Faso's line for 2022, and was rounded to the nearest 10 cents.3

The Development Economics topic reports the headline numbers; the interesting part is why they moved. The update raised the estimate of people in extreme poverty in 2022 by about 125 million, to around 838 million,4 with an extra 111 million in Sub-Saharan Africa. That does not mean the world suddenly became poorer. Several low-income countries had improved their household surveys, which now capture consumption more fully, for example food eaten outside the home. When measured consumption rises, countries also raise the thresholds that define poverty, so the international line rises too.

A line set by the poorest countries says little about poverty in richer ones. The World Bank therefore also publishes higher lines, now $4.20 a day for lower-middle-income countries and $8.30 for upper-middle-income countries, and it stresses that a country's own national line is far more appropriate for designing policy at home. Whenever you see a global poverty figure, check which line it uses.

concepts.title: The Elephant Curve and Its Critics
concepts.contentHtml:
In a 2013 World Bank working paper, Christoph Lakner and Branko Milanovic compiled national household surveys from 1988 to 2008 and plotted how much the real income of each part of the global distribution had grown. The curve rose high in the middle, sagged near the 80th percentile, then shot up again at the very top. Commentators named it the elephant curve after its shape.

Lakner and Milanovic described the winners as the groups that in 1988 sat around the median of the global distribution, 90% of whom lived in Asia,1 as China rose from the bottom ranks and created a global middle. The apparent losers sat around the 85th percentile in 1988, and almost 90% of them lived in mature economies: the lower middle class of the rich world. That reading fed a popular story about globalisation's losers in rich countries.

In 2016 Adam Corlett of the Resolution Foundation re-examined the data and found that much of the sag was a composition effect:

  • The set of countries in the data changed between 1988 and 2008. Using a consistent set raised measured global income growth from 24% to 32%.2
  • Populations grew fastest in poorer countries, a demographic headwind that was particularly strong around the global 70th to 85th percentiles.
  • The weak figures for rich countries were driven by Japan, partly through likely flawed data, and by Eastern European states whose incomes fell after the Soviet collapse. In the other mature economies, average real incomes grew 52%.3 The United States, with 41% growth unequally shared, came closest to the stagnation story.

The other side has not conceded. The World Inequality Report 2018 found the elephant even more marked: the global top 1% captured 27% of total growth from 1980 to 2016,4 twice the share captured by the bottom 50%. Lakner and Milanovic's global Gini index of about 70.5 for 2008 rises to almost 76 once surveys' under-reporting of top incomes is corrected, and its twenty-year fall then almost disappears. How much the rich world's middle lost, and why, is still argued.
